Its five-year correlation to the index says overlap, and its past-year capture readings say that overlap arrives magnified in both directions.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock is up 25% over the last five trading days, against 4.1% for the S&P 500. Runs like that pull money in. But the question that decides your wealth is not where this stock goes next week. It is how much of its return is genuinely its own story, and how much is the market you already own, arriving louder.

Marvell's 0.63 Correlation Is Overlap, Not A Separate Bet

Over the past five years, Marvell has returned 31% a year against the S&P 500's 13.4%, and its correlation to that index over the same window is 0.63, a high reading. A large part of what moves this stock is what moves the index fund you probably already hold. Gold returned 17.2% a year over those same five years, at a correlation to Marvell of 0.13, which is what a genuinely separate return stream looks like. Marvell has been the far better performer, but not the second engine. Since late June it has also been an S&P 500 constituent, so an S&P 500 index fund now owns some of it on your behalf, as do broad technology index funds.

Three Quarters Of Marvell's Revenue Now Rides One End Market

That absence of a separate story has a business explanation. The data center end market contributed 76% of the $2.418 billion Marvell booked in fiscal Q1 2027, sold as interconnect, switching and custom silicon. Management expects interconnect revenue alone to grow more than 70% year over year in fiscal 2027, and says only a handful of companies are driving the AI build-out it supplies. This is not a business cycle of its own; it is a concentrated position on how fast those few buyers keep spending. A return stream resting on one spending cycle is a structure the Trefis High Quality Portfolio deliberately avoids, since it does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its own returns.

Marvell Swings More Than Three Times The Market, In Both Directions

A 0.63 correlation still understates what this stock does to a portfolio. Marvell's annualized volatility over those five years was 64%, against 17.2% for the S&P 500. On days the index rose over the past year, Marvell captured about 356% of the market's gain; on days it fell, it absorbed about 307% of the loss. The tilt is favorable, but the scale is the point: for a year this has been the market's own direction with the volume turned up more than three times each way. The lived version is the past twelve months, in which the stock returned 194% and still sits about 31% below its 52-week high.

title: Intel Diversifies The Direction Of Your Returns, Not Their Size

Intel Diversifies The Direction Of Your Returns, Not Their Size

Image from Pixabay

Intel's moderate correlation to the market is partial independence, but the stock travels at more than three times the index's volatility.

Intel (INTC) stock is up 16.9% over the last five trading days while the S&P 500 gained 4.1%, and after a run like that the instinct is to buy more of what is working. The question that matters more to your money is how much of that return is Intel's own story rather than the index you already own, and what owning it does to your swings.

A 0.49 Correlation Is Independence Without Calm

Over the past five years Intel's daily moves carry a 0.49 correlation to the S&P 500, so it shares some of the market's direction while keeping a behavior of its own. That independence has come with a real return: 15.6% annualized against 13.4% for the index over the same five years. But correlation measures which way a stock travels, not how far. Intel's annualized volatility across that window was 54%, more than three times the index's. Gold, at a 0.15 correlation to Intel, returned 17.2% a year over the same stretch and out-earned Intel. Independence is not the scarce ingredient here; the size of Intel's own moves is.

Intel's Stock Answers To A Fab Calendar, Not An Economic One

One reason the overlap can stay moderate is what actually moves Intel: manufacturing execution. Intel 18A output ran roughly 25% above the company's own target in the second quarter of 2026; Panther Lake is ramping on that node, and management has committed to a high-volume ramp of Intel 14A in 2028. Intel Foundry's revenue in that same quarter was $5.8 billion, but only $293 million of the company's $16.1 billion in total revenue came from outside foundry customers, and management has raised the 2026 capital budget to more than $20 billion. Spending on that scale years ahead of the revenue is why the stock answers to Intel's timetable rather than the market's.

What Owning That Amplitude Costs When The Index Falls

Over the past year, a shorter window than the five-year figures above, Intel captured about 340% of the S&P 500's gain on up days and absorbed about 204% of the index's loss on down days. The asymmetry is favorable, and a single year can shift it. But the level is the point: on the days the index moves, this holding magnifies whatever the market is already doing to the rest of your portfolio. The down-day figure is the one that compounds against you, because recovering a large fall takes a gain much bigger than the fall itself, and blunting those falls is what the Trefis High Quality Portfolio is designed around.

title: How Intel's Earnings Turned AMD's Beat Into A Sell-Off
detail:
How Intel's Earnings Turned AMD's Beat Into A Sell-Off
Anusuya Lahiri
Wed, August 5, 2026 at 5:33 AM EDT 3 min read
AMD
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) stock fell nearly 9% in premarket trading Wednesday as investors appeared to want a stronger forward outlook following the chipmaker's second-quarter results.

The sell-off came even after AMD reported second-quarter revenue of $11.54 billion, topping the Wall Street estimate of $11.28 billion.

However, much of the market's attention shifted to the company's outlook, particularly expectations for Helios, its upcoming rack-scale AI platform.

Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman said the results "were good," but added that investors were looking for a "blowout guide driven by Helios."

AI Investment And Higher Expectations

The results also highlighted a sharp increase in investment spending. Capital expenditures rose to $808 million during the quarter from $282 million a year earlier and $389 million in the first quarter.

While the higher spending supports AMD's long-term AI expansion strategy, it may have weighed on near-term investor sentiment.

Adding to those expectations, AMD's results followed a strong quarterly report from Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC), raising the bar for investors evaluating the semiconductor sector.

AMD Results Look Solid Despite Stock Pressure

Bernstein senior analyst Stacy Rasgon said AMD delivered a solid quarter but may have fallen short of elevated investor expectations.

Rasgon, who has an Outperform rating and a $600 price forecast on AMD, told CNBC he saw nothing wrong with the results. He said revenue guidance and his earnings-per-share estimate were both above expectations, while gross margin was in line with forecasts.

He said investors may have been looking for more after Intel's strong report, even though AMD expects data center growth to accelerate in the second half of the year.

Analyst Sees AI Ramp And Strong Demand

Looking ahead, Rasgon said AMD's AI opportunity should expand further in the fourth quarter as the Helios platform ramps. He said the AI chip market remains large enough for AMD to grow alongside NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and other competitors.

He also said demand for server CPUs remains exceptionally strong, with customers buying as much supply as vendors can deliver. While Intel continues to sell products despite acknowledging competitive challenges, Rasgon said AMD has products that customers are actively seeking.

He said investors will be looking for more detail from AMD on the pace of data center growth, the Helios rollout, potential revenue contributions from Anthropic and the outlook for the company's client business.

The chipmaker's growth story is accelerating, but history offers a serious note of caution for anyone thinking of buying this pullback.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) is in the business of building the high-speed plumbing for the AI revolution. The company is all-in on data center infrastructure, from the optical interconnects that shuttle data between servers to the custom silicon that powers them. On its latest earnings call, management projected an acceleration in growth, forecasting revenue to climb approximately 40% this fiscal year and another 45% the next. Yet, even with that powerful narrative, the stock has recently pulled back about 22% from its 30-day high, and about 39% from its 52-week high. For an investor watching from the sidelines, that raises the essential question: is this a golden opportunity to buy into a growth story, or is it a trap?

What Happened After Past Marvell Technology Selloffs

When a hot stock stumbles, the first instinct is often to buy. But history suggests that for Marvell, it pays to be patient. The stock has seen 15 similar drops of 20% or more in a month since 2010. Looking at what happened next, the results are sobering. Only 6 of the 14 dips with a full year of subsequent data were followed by a positive return over the next year (the most recent, from July 2026, hasn't reached its one-year mark yet). The median 12-month return was -8%, though the table shows a median peak gain of 42% along the way (reached in a median 278 days) — the pain and the opportunity both showed up before the one-year mark. title: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Advanced Micro Devices vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Tue, August 4, 2026 at 3:59 PM EDT 6 min read
AMD
INTC
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The semiconductor landscape is shifting rapidly as artificial intelligence demands redefine hardware requirements for global enterprises. Choosing between Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) and Intel Corp (NASDAQ:INTC) requires understanding their different approaches to this massive technological transition.

Advanced Micro Devices has transformed from a secondary player into a leader in high-performance computing and AI accelerators. Intel, traditionally the dominant force in PC and server processors, is currently reorganizing its business to include foundry services and specialized AI chips. This comparison examines their financials, market strategies, and risks to help you determine which investment path is better.

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

Advanced Micro Devices designs high-performance and adaptive computing products, ranging from standard CPUs to advanced AI accelerators, within the semiconductor stocks category. It maintains essential relationships with cloud giants and console manufacturers like Sony Group Corp (NYSE:SONY) and Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT). Recently, the company partnered with OpenAI and Anthropic to deploy its latest GPU generations and acquired ZT Systems' design business to scale its infrastructure capabilities.

In FY 2025, revenue reached more than $34.6 billion, representing a significant 34% increase compared to the $25.8 billion recorded in the previous year. The company reported a net income of approximately $4.4 billion, which is a substantial rise from the $1.6 billion reported in 2024. Its net margin, which is the percentage of revenue left as profit, improved to roughly 12.5% during this period.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was a very low 0.1x, suggesting a conservative use of borrowed money. Free cash flow in 2025 was $5.5 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 21% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Intel Corp

Intel operates as an integrated device manufacturer, focusing on x86-based microprocessors and integrated graphics for PCs and data centers. The company also provides foundry services for semiconductor design, manufacturing, and assembly for external customers. It is currently navigating the complexities of its government-funded business model while managing high-profile shareholder lawsuits related to those deals.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $52.9 billion, a slight decrease of nearly 0.5% compared to the prior year. The company reported a net loss of close to $267 million for that fiscal period, though this was a marked improvement over the much larger loss in 2024. Its net margin was roughly negative 0.5%, reflecting the heavy research and manufacturing costs required to transform its business model.
